author: reek
body: Two things here are worth a test rather than a reading. The first is that a volume carries more than one FAT, and a writer that updates copy 0 and forgets copy 1 produces a disk that is wrong in a way nothing on this machine would notice -- our own reader consults copy 0. So the test asks copy 1 directly, and it asks it before and after, because an allocator that never wrote anything and one that wrote both copies both leave copy 0 and copy 1 in agreement if you only look once.

author: reek
body: The second is that the scan must not be stuck. block-sector-count returned 0 on every disk for as long as it existed and looked exactly like a working counter, because nothing ever demanded a specific number from it twice. So this test allocates, then scans again: the second free cluster must not be the first one. An allocator whose write silently did nothing returns the same cluster forever, and that is the failure this line is here to catch.
